bull_bear.body:
- ₹9/share FY26 dividend. GoI raised RE-subsidiary investment limit to ₹20,000 cr (supports 60 GW by 2032 target).
- Inorganic RE acquisitions explicitly flagged as a top-up lever.
- Possible value-unlock via listing of THDC/NEEPCO/Hindustan Urvarak — "no definitive plans," JV/policy-level decision.
- NGEL funded 80:20 debt:equity.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- RE-driven thermal backdown / falling PLF (regulated structure mitigates, but optics weigh on reported revenue).
- Transmission/GNA bottlenecks → curtailment (FY27 only 57% firm connectivity); T-GNA curtailment may rise before tapering.
- RE capacity slippage (FY26 5 GW plan spilled into FY27).
- Nuclear execution is long-dated (first power 2032) — optionality, not near-term earnings.
- One-off provisions (EESL/NBPPL/Garhi Dam) signal subsidiary/receivable risk.
- Lower competitive-bid wins in FY26 (NGEL stays away below threshold IRR) — pipeline replenishment dependent on MoUs.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Confident, granular, disciplined. Multi-year capacity/capex/connectivity/PPA breakdowns volunteered; explicit on RoE-protection mechanics; candid on pipeline normalization (32→30 GW) and bidding discipline. Receivable days improved 29→15. MSCI ESG upgraded CCC→BB. Tone reinforces regulated-compounder narrative.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- Flat top-line is a feature, not a bug: lower PLF cuts both fuel cost and sales while RoE/fixed charges hold — PAT +18% standalone despite revenue -2.69%.
- Co-located BESS at thermal plants turns the backdown problem into a peak-discharge revenue stream under cost-plus — a structural hedge against RE cannibalization.
- 14.5 GW non-solar connectivity application is an under-appreciated round-the-clock/FDRE land grab.
- Captive coal at ~18% (rising) materially de-risks fuel cost vs peers reliant on linkage/imports.
- NGEL EBITDA margin ~87% with generation +114% — the visible compounder inside the conglomerate.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- "Growth with Balanced Payouts" / "Balancing payout with deployment for growth plans", with the deck claiming the "Highest ever dividend payout on cash basis in FY26": dividend of ₹14,435 crore in FY26 against retained earnings of ₹10,564 crore, with payout ratios shown in the 38%-42% band.
- Group balance sheet at 31.03.2026: Group Debt ₹2,67,258 crore, Group Net Worth ₹2,03,024 crore and Group Regulated Equity ₹1,20,319 crore (up from ₹1,08,791 crore at 31.03.2025).
- Key ratios FY22 to FY26: Debt Equity 1.55, 1.50, 1.46, 1.34, 1.32; Leverage (Total Debt/EBITDA) 4.80, 4.37, 4.24, 4.19, 4.41; Total debt/total asset 0.50, 0.49, 0.49, 0.47, 0.48.
- Gross fixed assets grew to ₹4,70,618 crore in FY26 from ₹3,08,125 crore in FY22 at a stated CAGR of 11.17%; FY26 saw the "Highest Group Capex of ₹55,986 crore" and "Highest Group Profit of ₹27,546 crore".
- Trade receivables shown in days across 2021-22 to 2025-26 alongside the 100% realisation claim; group profit contribution includes Share of Profit from JVs of ₹2,864 crore and Profit of subsidiaries of ₹3,312 crore in FY26.
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- Scale: NTPC Group installed capacity of 89.1 GW as on 31 March 2026 (from 79.9 GW), the largest integrated power utility in India, generating 432.2 BU and contributing 23.6% of India's total power generation
- Execution: record capacity addition of ~9,618 MW in FY 2025-26 versus ~3,972 MW in FY 2024-25 (+142%), the highest-ever in a single year
- Operating efficiency: NTPC coal PLF of 72.0% against national coal PLF of 65.5%, an outperformance of ~6.47 percentage points; NTPC's coal plants continued to significantly outperform the national average
- Fuel security: 100% fuel tie-up for thermal capacity through long-term Fuel Supply Agreements with CIL and SCCL, with total Annual Contracted Quantity of 256.92 MMT across the NTPC group
- Backward integration into mining: 43.5 MMT of coal sourced from captive mines; captive coal production of 48.65 MMT (6.22% higher YoY), nearly 18% of annual requirement; NTPC Mining Limited is stated to be the third-largest coal mining company in India
- Import substitution: NTPC offset the shortfall from linked sources without procuring imported coal, thereby reducing the overall cost of power generation
- Pipeline depth: 34.2 GW under construction as on 31 March 2026 (versus 33.6 GW), maintaining a strong capacity pipeline even after record commissioning
- Diversification across the energy value chain via 11 subsidiaries, 17 joint ventures (including 2 international) and 9 step-down subsidiaries covering conventional and renewable generation, power trading, mining, nuclear, energy efficiency and engineering services
- Capital-markets standing: 33rd consecutive year of dividend declaration in FY 2025-26; a Board-formulated Dividend Distribution Policy under SEBI LODR Regulation 43A
- Leadership continuity and sector depth in the executive team (CMD with over 36 years in power and energy; functional directors with 35-37 years' experience each)
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Thermal utilisation structurally eroding as renewables displace coal — Stated as a Weakness in the MD&A SWOT: 'The increasing penetration of renewable energy has led to a decline in coal PLF (down by ~5 percentage points), impacting utilisation levels of thermal assets.' The SWOT bullet quantifies it as 'Coal PLF declining (-5.41 ppts) due to RE displacement'. This matters because the thermal fleet remains the bulk of NTPC's earning asset base and PLF drives fixed-cost recovery and incentive economics.
- Gas-based capacity (~4 GW) chronically underutilised — 'Gas-based capacity continues to remain underutilised, primarily due to fuel availability and pricing constraints.' A structural stranded-asset risk rather than a cyclical one, since it is driven by fuel supply and price rather than demand.
- Duck curve - daytime solar surplus with steep evening ramps — 'The increasing share of renewable energy (RE) introduces operational challenges, including the duck curve effect, characterised by periods of surplus solar generation and steep ramping requirements for thermal capacities.' Management notes the rate of increase in peak demand may surpass the rate of growth of energy demand, leading to sharper peaks from cooling load, data centre and EV demand 'which maybe difficult for coal plants to serve effectively'. Partial mitigation is stated: CERC tariff regulations offer a higher percentage of RoE for higher ramp-rate capability, and CEA's National Generation Adequacy Plan 2026 projects thermal capacity up to 315 GW by 2035-36, indicating continued need for coal-based reliability, ramping and reserve peaking.
- Grid integration complexity as variable RE penetration rises — 'Higher penetration of variable RE increases grid integration complexity, requiring enhanced flexibility, storage solutions, and system balancing capabilities.' Listed as a Threat in the SWOT matrix.
- Transmission bottlenecks in RE-rich states — Listed as a Threat: 'Transmission bottlenecks in RE-rich states (Rajasthan, Gujarat)'. A direct evacuation constraint on NTPC's own large solar and wind build-out, which is concentrated in exactly those geographies.
- Falling BESS tariffs making solar-plus-storage competitive against new thermal capacity — 'a downward trend in the BESS tariffs is also making solar + BESS more attractive to meet the non-solar hours peaking requirement, competing with new thermal capacities.' This is a competitive-obsolescence risk against the 16,520 MW of coal capacity NTPC currently has under construction.
- Daytime solar oversupply compressing market prices and raising price volatility — Stated as the threat to the Group's own high-growth RE plans: 'For the high-growth plans of RE capacity addition by NTPC Group, the threat is in form of excess solar supply during day-time compressing market prices and causing high price volatility through the da[y]'. NOTE: this sentence is TRUNCATED mid-word at the end of the MD&A section, so the remainder of management's statement on this risk is not available in the routed text.
- Foreign currency exposure on borrowings and procurement contracts — Managed through a defined Exchange Risk Management Policy including hedging instruments; during FY 2025-26 the Company entered into derivative contracts aggregating JPY 15,989.65 million, USD 487.66 million and EUR 12.89 million towards management of foreign currency loan exposures. The scale of hedging activity indicates a material FCY-denominated funding base.
- Board composition non-compliance - independent directors below the mandated number — BACK-FILLED: this risk belongs to the risks domain but appears only in the sibling governance_entities and profile bundles (Corporate Governance Report, section 2.1), not in the risks_esg bundle. Against an approved composition of eight Independent Directors, as on 31 March 2026 the Board had only five; 'During FY 2025-26, numbers of Independent Directors were less than half of the Board' and 'the mandates regarding the presence of a woman independent director and at least 50% non-executive directors were not fulfilled until 18th May 2025'. NTPC has requested the Ministry of Power to make the necessary appointments. A standing SEBI LODR / DPE compliance exposure that the Company cannot itself remedy, since all directors are appointed by the President of India.

business.title: Challenges → beneficiaries & losers

business.body:
- "Largest Power Generator in India" with operational capacity of over 90 GW, ~24% share in electricity generated with ~17% share in installed capacity (share of installed capacity as on 31 March 2026; share of electricity generated during FY26).
- Vision is "To be the world's Leading Power Company, accelerating India's Growth & Energy Transition"; the concluding slide frames the case as Integrated Power Major, Future-ready Energy Portfolio, Strong Operational and Financial Fundamentals, Disciplined Capital Allocation, Clear and Ambitious Growth Roadmap, Sustainable Value Creation and Committed to the vision of Viksit Bharat.
- Sector backdrop cited: India's total installed capacity of 549 GW at June 2026 (+13% YoY from 485 GW), non-fossil 297 GW including 237 GW RE (+22% YoY from 243 GW) and solar 162 GW (+40% YoY from 116 GW); India's per-capita electricity is "roughly a third of the world average and a tenth of the US level".
- Payment security is a structural moat: "Regulatory framework assuring returns with balancing risks and rewards", Tri-Partite Agreements plus LC mechanism and Late Payment Surcharge Rules 2022, with "100% Realization (~₹1.56 Lakh Crore) during FY26".
- Global footprint via BIFPCL Bangladesh (50:50 JV with BPDB; 1320 MW thermal operational since 2022 under a G2G framework, plus a 2x660 MW coal-based project with USD 2 Bn investment), TPCL Sri Lanka (50:50 JV with EGL; 50 MW + 70 MW solar, commissioning expected FY28, ~USD 43 Mn phase-I), NMEL Mauritius (wholly owned; 15 MW floating solar PV with 12/48 MWhr BESS, ~USD 30 Mn) and consultancy (PMC contracts for 6.6 GW awarded under the International Solar Alliance).
business.title: Positioning (investor deck)

business.body:
- [Restructuring] "Transfer of Coal Mining Business to NTPC Mining Ltd completed on 01st April 2026" — the captive coal business now sits in a separate entity.
- [Unit label conflict] The capacity slide header reads "Portfolio Capacity-126.61 MW" while the accompanying table and the sibling header ("Under Operation-90.9 GW") are in GW; both readings are reproduced as printed rather than reconciled.
- [Group vs standalone] FY26 results are presented on both bases and must not be conflated: consolidated EBITDA ₹60,564 crore versus standalone EBITDA ₹49,030 crore; Group Profit ₹27,546 crore versus standalone "Profit for the period" of ₹23,162 crore.
- [Workplace recognition] Recognised as one of the 'Best Organizations to Work 2026' by ET Edge, ranked 2nd in 'Future-Ready Workplaces' 2025 by Fortune India & CIEL HR, and Most Preferred Workplace 2025-26 by Team Marksmen.
- [Demand outlook] Projected electricity requirement rises from 1,708 Bn units in FY26 toward FY50 and FY70 scenario levels, with peak demand and per-capita consumption (1,460 kWh/year in FY25 versus a 3,900 world average and 13,000 in the US) sourced from the NITI Aayog "Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero" report.
business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: NTPC is among India's largest integrated energy conglomerates, with a presence across the energy value chain and a growing portfolio of conventional and renewable energy assets. The Group generates and sells electricity from coal, gas, hydro, renewable and pumped-storage capacity to distribution utilities and other beneficiaries under a payment-security framework of Letters of Credit and Tri-Partite Agreements, and complements this through subsidiaries and joint ventures engaged in power trading, captive coal mining, nuclear energy, energy efficiency, engineering services and allied businesses. Its captive mining arm NTPC Mining Limited operates coal mines that supply the thermal fleet, and its trading arm NVVN handles power trading, rooftop/ground-mounted solar, waste-to-energy and carbon management.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Four stated growth priorities: meeting India's rising electricity demand; strengthening energy security through domestic capabilities; expanding clean and flexible energy infrastructure; and leveraging digital technologies to improve efficiency and reliability.
- Clean energy transition strategy anchored on a corporate plan targeting 149 GW of total installed capacity by 2032 including 60 GW from renewable energy, with a further aspiration of reaching 244 GW by 2037.
- Scale and efficiency in the core: continued focus on scale, efficiency and clean energy expansion to make the business model resilient to changing sector dynamics.
- Retain and upgrade the thermal fleet rather than exit it - investments in emission control systems, flexible operations, biomass co-firing, water conservation, ash utilisation and carbon management to make thermal assets more efficient and environmentally responsible.
- Fuel self-reliance through captive mining: NTPC Mining Limited operating six mines with three under development, with captive coal production supplying nearly 18% of annual requirement.
- Build out storage: expand pumped storage projects and battery energy storage systems, plus investment in next-generation long-duration storage technologies including CO2-based energy storage systems and vanadium redox flow batteries.
- Enter and scale nuclear: entry via the Mahi Banswara project in Rajasthan, with studies across 34 sites in 13 States and a site selection report for one location submitted to the Department of Atomic Energy.
- Digital-first operations: integrate artificial intelligence, predictive analytics and advanced forecasting across generation, renewable, mining and maintenance operations to improve plant availability, optimise operations, reduce costs and strengthen safety; ICT initiatives during FY26 included Wagon Tippler-Safe Operation, Demand-based Coal Planning and Cost Optimisation, Advanced Pattern Recognition, AI-generated synopses of e-Office files, Automated Summary Sheets and 'Talk to Document - Jyotibot'.
- Strengthen enterprise risk management: ERM framework revised in July 2025 to align with ISO 31000:2018, overseen by a Board-level Risk Management Committee; first CPSE in the power sector to implement a Business Continuity Plan aligned with ISO 22301:2019.
- Manage FX exposure under a defined Exchange Risk Management Policy using hedging instruments for foreign-currency borrowings and procurement contracts.
- Human capital strategy under the Employee Value Proposition 'People before PLF', built on four pillars of Competence, Commitment, Culture and Systems Building, focused on leadership development, succession planning, continuous learning, engagement and digital transformation.
- Governance and integrity: vigilance function certified under ISO 9001 and ISO 37001, digitalisation of vigilance processes, revision of the Whistle Blower Policy and continued use of the Integrity Pact for eligible procurement contracts.
- NTPC's stated capital-allocation posture combines an uninterrupted dividend record with debt-funded growth. For FY 2025-26 the 50th AGM notice asks members to confirm two interim dividends of 27.50% each (Rs 2.75 per equity share of Rs 10 each) already paid, and to declare a final dividend of 35% (Rs 3.50 per equity share) recommended by the Board and payable out of the profits of the year. Funding intent is explicit: during FY 2025-26 shareholders passed a special resolution by postal ballot (23 July 2025) authorising the raising of funds up to Rs 18,000 crore through issue of Non-Convertible Debentures / Bonds on a private placement basis. BACK-FILLED from the sibling profile bundle (Directors' Report sections 2 and 3): the Board has formulated a Dividend Distribution Policy in terms of Regulation 43A of SEBI (LODR) Regulations, 2015, which is published on the Company's website; FY 2025-26 was the 33rd consecutive year of dividend declaration; and during the year the Company issued two tranches of unsecured, rated, listed, non-cumulative, non-convertible redeemable debentures of Rs 4,000 crore each (6.84% Series-83-2035 and 6.89% Series-84-2035) on private placement, with the funds utilised for the purpose for which they were raised and no deviations or variations in utilisation. IMPORTANT GAP: the section headed '=== DIVIDEND DISTRIBUTION POLICY ===' in this bundle does not contain the policy at all - the actual dividend-policy terms (trigger factors, payout parameters, retention criteria) were not routed and are therefore not captured here. Payout-ratio and dividend-amount figures that appear in the Directors' Report financial-summary table have been deliberately excluded as profit-derived financial-statement content.
- Ash utilisation: NTPC Group achieved a record ~106% ash utilisation in FY26 (106.2 million MT ash processed), stated as leadership in circular resource management.
- Green hydrogen hub: a 1,200-acre green hydrogen hub at Pudimadaka, Andhra Pradesh with foundation stone laid by the Prime Minister; key infrastructure work underway; the project is expected to utilise 7 GW of RE-RTC in its final phase and export up to 2.5 MMTPA of green hydrogen derivatives (green hydrogen, green ammonia, e-methanol, SAF).
- Green fuel pilots at Pudimadaka: Green Ethanol (10 TPD), Sustainable Aviation Fuel (6 TPD) and Green Urea (150 TPD).
- Green ammonia: NTPC is the first CPSE to set up a Green Ammonia project (70,000 TPA capacity) won under the ambit of the National Green Hydrogen Mission.
- Hydrogen blending and mobility: Green hydrogen-PNG blending project at Kawas commissioned, achieving 8% vol/vol blending; the world's highest-altitude green hydrogen fuelling station at Leh, Ladakh, leading to India's first commercial operation of hydrogen FCEV buses; India's largest green hydrogen fuelling station at Greater NOIDA for five hydrogen FCEVs in intercity mode; a solar hydrogen-based microgrid with the Indian Army at Chushul, Ladakh at 4,400 m above mean sea level, stated as the world's highest-altitude green hydrogen project.
- Battery energy storage: the Ministry of Power allocated 5 GWh of BESS capacity (letter dated 09.06.2025) to be installed at NTPC power stations under the VGF scheme via the Power System Development Fund at Rs 18 lakh/MWh; NTPC has identified 16 thermal power projects for 5 GWh aggregate (15 projects of 4.7 GWh at NTPC stations and one 0.3 GWh project at NTECL Vallur); MoP sanctioned a VGF grant of Rs 900 crore on 12.01.2026.
- Pumped storage: THDC's Tehri Pumped Storage Project delivered the Group's first commercial PSP capacity with three units of 250 MW each commissioned in FY 2025-26 and the fourth and last 250 MW unit commissioned on 12 April 2026; the Group has a PSP portfolio of over 18 GW, with 4,800 MW allocated from NTPC to NTECL, THDC and NEEPCO, plus direct allocations to THDC (10,110 MW) and NEEPCO (2,100 MW) under various stages of execution.
- Nuclear as a decarbonisation vehicle: ASHVINI, the 51:49 joint venture between NPCIL and NTPC, received Government approval to build, own and operate nuclear power plants; the 4x700 MW Mahi Banswara Rajasthan Atomic Power Project was transferred to ASHVINI with AERB siting and excavation consents, environmental clearance transfer, asset transfer agreement, equity infusion of Rs 800 crore by JV partners and foundation stone laying by the Prime Minister; more than 30 potential sites identified; SMR opportunities pursued with HOLTEC, USA; a Coal-to-Nuclear feasibility study completed for repurposing older thermal stations; overseas uranium asset opportunities explored with UCIL; aligned to the Government's 100 GW nuclear capacity roadmap by 2047.
- Waste-to-energy / circular economy: the Varanasi Harit Koyla Pariyojna, India's first Waste-to-Charcoal plant, processes 600 TPD of MSW/RDF into ~150 TPD of torrefied charcoal (green coal) using an indigenous, oxygen-limited torrefaction process aligned with Swachh Bharat and Atmanirbhar Bharat; NTPC completed the buyout of MCD's 26% equity stake in NTPC EDMC Waste Solutions Pvt. Ltd. as of May 2026, making it wholly owned, with NVVN's WtE assets proposed to be transferred to it.
- E-mobility: e-buses are operational across Andaman & Nicobar and Bengaluru under NTPC's ambit, with cumulative running kilometres continuing to grow.
- Carbon markets: 28.6 million carbon credits generated, with more pending (stated as an Opportunity in the SWOT).
- Offshore wind: NTPC Group is actively exploring offshore wind opportunities, leveraging emerging policy support and global partnerships to diversify its renewable portfolio.
- CSR: Rs 526.98 crore actualised (including set-off) towards CSR during FY 2025-26 against a statutory CSR obligation of Rs 411.98 crore; programmes benefitted more than 1,000 villages and over 1,400 schools, impacting around 22 lakh people. The Girl Empowerment Mission (GEM) ran across 42 stations for Summer Workshop 2026, having grown from three locations and 392 participants in 2018 to 17 states and over 16,000 young girls. Flagship programmes are also run through the NTPC Foundation.
- Rehabilitation & Resettlement: guided by the R&R Policy, 2017 aligned with the 2013 Land Acquisition Act; over the last ten years NTPC has incurred more than Rs 2,682 crore on community development works under various R&R Plans; R&R and community development continued across thermal, hydro and coal mining projects in FY 2025-26.
- R&D for the transition: Rs 583.20 crore of R&D expenditure in FY 2025-26 through NETRA, focused on Carbon Capture Utilisation and Storage (CCUS), green hydrogen, advanced energy storage, coal gasification, ash utilisation technologies, waste-to-energy and renewable integration.
- Risk-governance certifications: ERM framework revised in July 2025 to align with ISO 31000:2018 under a Board-level Risk Management Committee; NTPC states it is the first CPSE in the power sector to implement a comprehensive Business Continuity Plan aligned with ISO 22301:2019.
- ESG ratings: the Company states 'sustained improvement in ESG performance and sustainability initiatives, as evidenced by significant upgrades in its ratings from several reputed agencies' - the agencies and the rating levels are NOT named in the routed text.
- NO BRSR SECTION WAS ROUTED TO THIS BUNDLE. No BRSR principle-wise disclosures, no material responsible-business-conduct issues table, no emissions / energy / water / waste intensity data and no diversity or safety statistics are present. The ESG items above come from the MD&A green-business narrative and the Directors' Report CSR, R&R, NETRA and Risk Management sections only, and should not be read as NTPC's full ESG disclosure.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: FY 2025-26 was NTPC's largest build year since inception. On a standalone basis the Company added 1,823 MW to reach 60,796 MW as at 31 March 2026 (against 59,413 MW a year earlier), after permanently discontinuing operations of 440 MW at Tanda Stage-I with effect from 1 September 2025. At the Group level 9,618 MW was added - including 7,795 MW by subsidiaries and joint ventures - taking Group installed capacity to 89,108 MW from 79,930 MW; Group commercial capacity rose to 87,977 MW, an addition of 8,488 MW. The long-term Corporate Plan aims for 60 GW of renewable energy capacity and 149 GW of total installed capacity (and 1 GW PSP) by 2032, and 244 GW of total installed capacity (and 6.2 GW of PSP) by 2037, pursued through both organic and inorganic expansion across thermal, hydro, renewable and nuclear. As on 31 March 2026, projects aggregating 34,188 MW were under implementation, of which 20,615 MW sits in subsidiaries and joint ventures; the under-construction portfolio comprises 16,520 MW of coal-based projects (12,520 MW at NTPC, 4,000 MW at subsidiaries/JVs), 2,631 MW of hydro (811 MW at NTPC, 1,820 MW at subsidiaries/JVs) and 15,037 MW of renewable energy (242 MW at NTPC, 14,795 MW at subsidiaries/JVs). In hydro, the Group has 4,475 MW of operational hydropower capacity and is expanding through the 2,631 MW under implementation. In nuclear, the flagship is the Mahi Banswara Rajasthan Atomic Power Project (4 x 700 MW), executed through the strategic vehicle ASHVINI (the NTPC-NPCIL joint venture) with NTPC Parmanu Urja Nigam Limited (NPUNL) as the dedicated nuclear subsidiary; approximately 34 potential sites across multiple states have been identified, with Small Modular Reactors and advanced fuels as emerging technologies and capability development through BARC, NPCIL, IGCAR and international collaborations, aligned to India's 100 GW nuclear vision by 2047. In renewables, commissioned capacity as on 31 March 2026 was 11,547 MW (10,654 MW solar and 893 MW wind), with 15,040 MW under execution (9,403 MW solar and 5,637 MW wind), supported by investments in utility-scale solar, wind, hybrid projects and Ultra Mega Renewable Energy Power Parks. Under National Solar Mission Phase-I, for which NTPC through NVVN was nodal agency, commissioned capacity stood at 733 MW with 4,941 million units of bundled solar power supplied during FY 2025-26. In distributed renewables, 61.72 MW of rooftop solar had been commissioned through NVVN under RESCO and PMC models for Central Ministries, Government Departments and public institutions, with a further 139 MW under implementation and 22.62 MW under tendering. In waste-to-energy, the 600 TPD Varanasi Waste-to-Charcoal project was commissioned during FY 2025-26, producing over 3,000 tonnes of green charcoal supplied to NTPC Unchahar for co-firing; further plants are under implementation at Bhopal (400 TPD), Hubballi-Dharwad (200 TPD), Noida-Greater Noida (900 TPD) and Gorakhpur (500 TPD), development has been initiated at Meerut (900 TPD), and project-management support is being extended to upcoming facilities at Gurugram and Faridabad. Commercially, the Company achieved 100% realisation of bills due for collection under a payment-security framework of Letters of Credit and Tri-Partite Agreements, and sold a record 8,285 MU through power exchanges. Projects are executed through an Integrated Project Management and Control System (IPMCS) covering Engineering Management, Quality Assurance & Inspection, Contract Management and Site Management Control Centres, aimed at timely commissioning within approved cost parameters. NOTE ON AN INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY IN THE AR: the Directors' Report states 15,037 MW of renewable projects under implementation while the Group overview section states 15,040 MW under execution (9,403 MW solar + 5,637 MW wind); both are reproduced above as stated and neither has been reconciled or adjusted.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's electricity demand is projected to grow at 6-6.5% per annum, significantly higher than the global average of approximately 2.8%, driven by rising industrialization, urbanization, digitalization and improving standards of living.
- Peak demand crossed 270 GW in FY26 and is projected by CEA to reach about 459 GW by FY36; the National Generation Adequacy Plan 2026 projects electricity demand of ~3365 BU by FY 2035-36, underscoring continued requirement for substantial capacity additions.
- The rapid expansion of AI, cloud computing and data centres will increase demand for reliable, high-quality, round-the-clock power; expansion in manufacturing, infrastructure, electric mobility, urbanisation and digital services is expected to sustain growth.
- Renewables are structurally displacing coal: NTPC Group generation was 432.2 BU in FY 2025-26, marginally lower than 438.6 BU in FY 2024-25, primarily reflecting the national trend of RE displacing coal generation during solar-rich periods and a stronger early monsoon reducing thermal dispatch.
- India's thermal generation declined about 4% and coal-based generation about 3.7% in FY 2025-26, while RE generation (including hydro) grew ~18%, led by solar (~20%) and wind (~27%); gas-based generation declined ~18%.
- Storage economics are inflecting: global battery pack costs dropped 45% Y-o-Y to nearly $70/kWh in 2025, reducing levelized cost of storage and driving capacity additions; CEA expects India to add ~174 GW / 888 GWh of storage capacity by 2035.
- Counterparty health is improving: the DISCOM ACS-ARR gap narrowed to Rs 0.06/kWh in FY 2024-25 from Rs 0.21/kWh in FY 2023-24, AT&C losses fell to 15.04%, and legacy dues declined from Rs 1,39,947 crore in 2022 to Rs 3,330 crore by March 2026 under the amended Late Payment Surcharge Rules.
- Regulatory tailwinds for storage and nuclear: CERC Tariff Regulations (Second Amendment) 2026 created a framework for Energy Storage Systems co-located with thermal plants and ISTS with defined norms (battery life 15 years, RoE 14%, availability 90%, efficiency >=85%); the SHANTI Act, 2025 permits private and foreign participation (up to 49% FDI) in nuclear; customs duty exemption on nuclear project imports extended until 2035.
- Demand-side mandates: the Renewable Consumption Obligation raises renewable consumption targets from ~30% in FY 2024-25 to ~43% by FY 2029-30 for DISCOMs, open access consumers and captive users, while RGO compliance has been made voluntary for thermal stations commissioned after April 2025, giving greater flexibility in renewable capacity planning.
- Thermal flexibility economics: the CERC Order of October 2025 allows thermal generating units to undertake unit shutdown when scheduled below 50% of capacity, improving operational efficiency.
- Cost tailwind for renewables build-out: GST on renewable equipment reduced from 12% to 5%, with REEIMS launched and incentives for domestic battery manufacturing.
- Long-run sector investment thesis: NITI Aayog's February 2026 report projects electricity at nearly 60% of total energy consumption by 2070, non-fossil at about 98% of power generation, and cumulative power-sector investment of approximately USD 14.2 trillion through 2070.
- With around 35 GW of projects under construction, NTPC has a strong growth pipeline for the coming years (Chairman & Managing Director's letter).
- Under Construction capacity of 34.2 GW as on 31 March 2026 versus 33.6 GW a year earlier - 'Maintaining strong capacity pipeline even after record capacity commissioning' (MD&A segment-wise performance table).
- NTPC is a power utility and does not disclose a conventional order book; the pipeline above is the capacity-under-construction disclosure and is the closest equivalent stated in the routed text.

risks.note: Stated as a Weakness in the MD&A SWOT: 'The increasing penetration of renewable energy has led to a decline in coal PLF (down by ~5 percentage points), impacting utilisation levels of thermal assets.' The SWOT bullet quantifies it as 'Coal PLF declining (-5.41 ppts) due to RE displacement'. This matters because the thermal fleet remains the bulk of NTPC's earning asset base and PLF drives fixed-cost recovery and incentive economics.
risks.risk: Thermal utilisation structurally eroding as renewables displace coal

risks.note: 'Gas-based capacity continues to remain underutilised, primarily due to fuel availability and pricing constraints.' A structural stranded-asset risk rather than a cyclical one, since it is driven by fuel supply and price rather than demand.

'The increasing share of renewable energy (RE) introduces operational challenges, including the duck curve effect, characterised by periods of surplus solar generation and steep ramping requirements for thermal capacities.' Management notes the rate of increase in peak demand may surpass the rate of growth of energy demand, leading to sharper peaks from cooling load, data centre and EV demand 'which maybe difficult for coal plants to serve effectively'. Partial mitigation is stated: CERC tariff regulations offer a higher percentage of RoE for higher ramp-rate capability, and CEA's National Generation Adequacy Plan 2026 projects thermal capacity up to 315 GW by 2035-36, indicating continued need for coal-based reliability, ramping and reserve peaking.
risks.risk: Duck curve - daytime solar surplus with steep evening ramps

risks.note: 'Higher penetration of variable RE increases grid integration complexity, requiring enhanced flexibility, storage solutions, and system balancing capabilities.' Listed as a Threat in the SWOT matrix.
risks.risk: Grid integration complexity as variable RE penetration rises

risks.note: Listed as a Threat: 'Transmission bottlenecks in RE-rich states (Rajasthan, Gujarat)'. A direct evacuation constraint on NTPC's own large solar and wind build-out, which is concentrated in exactly those geographies.

'a downward trend in the BESS tariffs is also making solar + BESS more attractive to meet the non-solar hours peaking requirement, competing with new thermal capacities.' This is a competitive-obsolescence risk against the 16,520 MW of coal capacity NTPC currently has under construction.
risks.risk: Falling BESS tariffs making solar-plus-storage competitive against new thermal capacity

risks.note: Stated as the threat to the Group's own high-growth RE plans: 'For the high-growth plans of RE capacity addition by NTPC Group, the threat is in form of excess solar supply during day-time compressing market prices and causing high price volatility through the da[y]'. NOTE: this sentence is TRUNCATED mid-word at the end of the MD&A section, so the remainder of management's statement on this risk is not available in the routed text.
risks.risk: Daytime solar oversupply compressing market prices and raising price volatility

risks.note: Managed through a defined Exchange Risk Management Policy including hedging instruments; during FY 2025-26 the Company entered into derivative contracts aggregating JPY 15,989.65 million, USD 487.66 million and EUR 12.89 million towards management of foreign currency loan exposures. The scale of hedging activity indicates a material FCY-denominated funding base.
risks.risk: Foreign currency exposure on borrowings and procurement contracts

sk.overview: The DRHP frames the issuer's industry through a CRISIL-commissioned report titled "Assessment of Indian power and renewable energy market" (July 2026). meta.thesis: RoE-protected regulated utility compounding on record capacity adds (group >90 GW), where flat revenue masks 18% standalone / 15% group PAT growth because fixed-charge recovery insulates the bottom line from RE-driven thermal backdowns — with embedded optionality in NGEL, BESS, PSP and nuclear.
